name: Ontario Violet
lede: Ontario Violet is a light, greyed blue-violet named for Ontario, Canada's most populous province, and recorded as a color standard since 1912.

sections.title: A province's name
sections.body:
Ontario became a Canadian province at Confederation in 1867, taking its name from the lake on its southern border, itself said to come from an Iroquoian word for a large or beautiful lake [3]. Ridgway's 1912 standards plate this violet-blue on plate XXXVI, hue 55 double-prime, tone b [1]. The ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 later filed the same swatch, block 203, as a pale purplish blue, 3.4 units from that block's center[1]. Maerz and Paul give 1912 as its first recorded use and the Munsell notation 7.7PB 6.3/5.7 [1].

Its nearest named neighbors are Chicory Blue, 4.0 units away, and Light Dull Bluish Violet, 4.2 units away [1]. It sits between the families of [[blue]] and [[violet]], close to [[chicory-blue]] and [[blue-bell]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Ontario Violet covers at least five percent of the canvas in 56 works, under a quarter of one percent[2]. The earliest dated example is Piero della Francesca's 1474 portrait of Battista Sforza, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. It peaks in the 1890s, in 11 of 1,173 paintings, nearly four times the archive's overall rate for that decade, and it turns up in Post-Impressionist paintings here almost nineteen times the baseline rate [2]. It shares a canvas with [[periwinkle]] far more than any other color word, over a hundred times the baseline[2]. These are screen-color matches on photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not pigment identifications [2]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[2].
